utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'd like to greet Mr. Scott, the Defence, the accused, and the Ambassador, whose testimony will be completed today. We'll continue with the cross-examination now. But as far as time is concerned, I'd like to point out the following: We'll have the cross-examination for one and a half hours, and then we will have a 20-minute break. We will then resume our work, which would bring us up to 1.15 or 1.20. We will then have a one-hour break for administrative reasons and to allow everyone to have lunch, and we will resume our work again around 2.15 or 2.20, and I hope that the cross-examination and re-examination will be completed by about 4.00 p.m. This should then give time to the accused to address certain procedural matters. And we should adjourn by 5.00 p.m. at the latest, I hope. I will now give the Defence the floor to continue with the -- the cross-examination. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Cross-examination by the Accused Praljak:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Ambassador. According to my calculations, I have another 35 minutes, but could that please be checked, and I think I will be granted a few additional minutes. Before I start with the cross-examination, could we have 3D 00873 on the screen. It's in the e-court system it. And while waiting for it to appear on the screen, I will put the following question to the ambassador: Ambassador, I will now mention certainly international peace initiatives and the plans that were put before the warring factions, the warring parties. There is the Cutileiro Plan, March 1992; then the Vance-Owen Plan, 1992, 1993. This plan evolved. Then there is the proposal of the international community on the structure of Bosnia and Herzegovina as the union of three republics. Geneva, the 20th of August, 1993, and then we have the Washington Agreement dated the 1st of March, 1994. Then there's the Contact Group plan on the internal structure of -- of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was to be composed of two entities, Geneva July 4 1994 is the date, and then we have the Dayton agreement the 10th of November, 1995. Ambassador, are these the proposals that the international community put on the table before the warring factions in Bosnia-Herzegovina during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are. You have omitted two plans. One was called the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan, and the other was called the Invincible Plan, named after the British warship on which it was concluded, but basically your outline is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Invincible. So that was on the Invincible warship. My question is quite simple. As far as all these proposals are concern, did the Croatian side sign first and did never withdrew its signature?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, I hear you in Serbo-Croatian and read you in English, but I do not have the English coming through my microphone. Could that be adjusted? I've pushed all the buttons and it doesn't help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Number 4.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you speak, General, just so we test the system? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good day. Good day.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hear you in Serbo-Croatian. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One, two.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two, two.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It's fine now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So my question was as follows --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, your questions as far as these proposals are concerned, did the Croatian first and never withdraw its agreement. That is the case that I know of for Cutileiro and the Vance-Owen Plan. I wasn't involved with the others, so I can't be sure. So I don't know about the others. The answer, as far as the Cutileiro Plan of March 1992 and the Vance-Owen Plan of January 1993, is that the Croatian side signed first.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So could we draw the following conclusion: Dayton, and you as a political analyst are well aware of the fact we were given a divided state. We had the Federation on the one side and the Republika Srpska with 49 per cent of the territory on the other side. Would that be correct according to the information that you have?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm well aware of Dayton. The Dayton plan partitioned the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina about in half with the Federation of Croats and Muslims being granted 51 per cent and the Republika Srpska 49 per cent. That is of the territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you also aware of the following fact: When a census was taken in 1991 in the territory of Republika Srpska less than 10 per cent of Croats -- or 10 per cent less of Croats lived in the area than was the case before, and about -- there were about 85 per cent of Bosniaks who didn't live in the territory of Republika Srpska any more.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of those exact figures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on to the next question. It's in relation to Bill Clinton's book, "My Life." Have you had this book in your hands?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's not that important. There are certain political ideas that he expresses here. Could we first see 3D 00873. 3D 00873. That's the book. And now 3D 00856. 3D 00856. In his book the American president Bill Clinton, and this can be seen in the pages that have been translated into English, says the following -- first I'll read out certain paragraphs, and then I'll ask you whether you agree with his political assessments and with the facts expressed here. At the very beginning it says that Slobodan Milosevic seemed to be withdrawing his army from Bosnia, whereas weapons, supplies, and Bosnian Serbs were left under the control of commander Ratko Mladic. Fights and killings continued during 1992. The European Community leaders were restrained while the Bush's government was rather insecure as to what should be done, and it was also indecisive and could not decide to enter into new problems in the year of an election, so it left these problems to be solved by the European Community. However, the Bush government stood by the European Community in order to impose economic sanctions on Serbia, and measures that General-Secretary Boutros Boutros-Ghali, the French, and the British tried to resist initially, and then we'll skip a few lines, and then Mr. Clinton says the following: "The problem with the embargo was that the Serbs had a sufficient amount of weapons and ammunition to fight a war for years." And could we now see page 489 of the Croatian translation where it says at the beginning of February I decide the not to support the Vance-Owen Plan, and it since and reads as follows: "A few days later on, we concluded -- we completed a new proposal for Bosnian policies, and Warren Christopher said that the United States wanted to discuss new agreement." And then on the same page it continues to read as follows: "On the 9th of the very same month, at our first meeting the French president Francois Mitterrand informed me that although he had sent 5.000 French soldiers to Bosnia as part of the UN humanitarian forces, he was more in favour of the Serbs than I was and he was less willing to see a united Bosnia under the control of the Muslims." And then it says: "I met with Helmut Kohl on the 26th of March. He complained about the events and, like myself, was in favour of revoking the weapons embargo. However, we were unable to convince the French and the British who believed that without the embargo, the war would only be prolonged and the UN forces would be in jeopardy. And then it says, in April, and we're talking about 1993, the American team for military and diplomatic and humanitarian aid returned from Bosnia with the request that we should become militarily engaged in order to put an end to the slaughter. Now I'll skip a few sentences. "By the end of the month the team for foreign policy suggested that if we couldn't convince the Serbs to stop the killing we would have to withdraw or revoke the embargo on weapons for the Muslims and start launching airstrikes targeting Serbian military targets." And then in the following paragraph it says: "The end of the first 100-day period we weren't even close to finding a satisfactory solution to the crisis in Bosnia. The British and the French didn't accept Warren Christopher's suggestions, and they reaffirmed their right to be the key players in finding a solution to the problem." And then finally I will read out the following in the last paragraph: "I ended up in a situation that Dick Holbrooke called one of the biggest collective failures of safety in the West since the '30s. In his book Holbrooke said five factors contributed to failure: Firstly, misinterpretation of the history of the Balkans; secondly, the obvious loss of the strategic the importance of Yugoslavia after the end of the Cold War; and, thirdly, the victory of nationalism over democracy as the dominant ideology of post-communist Yugoslavia; four, the unwillingness of Bush's government to be involved in another military action immediately after the war in Iraq, and five, the US decision to let Europe deal with this issue instead of NATO, and confuse and --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. This statement has now gone on for some seven minutes, seven minutes. I wonder if we're getting to a question. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Naturally we will get to a question. It's not a statement. I'm just reading out something, and you have done the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm objecting, Your Honour, at this point. I'm objecting to the continued reading out of this material, and if Mr. Praljak has a question, he should go straight to his question, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you've enumerated the five items mentioned by Mr. Holbrooke, so go ahead and put your question to the witness since the Ambassador has also had ample time to read out Bill Clinton's text. So you can put your question to him right now. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I have just two more sentences, Your Honours. "I would add a sixth factor to Holbrooke's list. Some European unions do not want to have a Muslim state in the heart of the Balkans and they fear it might become a base to which extremism is imported, although the result of their neglect was rather similar." And that's the end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, could you tell me the following -- or, rather, could you tell the Chamber the following: Did Mr. Bill Clinton directly enumerate the problems that you also became aware of in relation to the way in which these peace plans were submitted and developed, the peace plans for Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of his analysis is correct. Part is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you briefly tell us which part of the analysis is incorrect?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The part that's incorrect first is his rejection of the Vance-Owen Plan. You will notice in the book, which I'm seeing for the first time as we mentioned earlier, that he gives no reasons for rejection by the United States of the Vance-Owen Plan. That itself is significant. The silence speaks very loudly. With regard to the points he gives quoting Holbrooke, the first point is incorrect. There was no historical misinterpretation of the situation by the negotiators. The press often spoke about ancient hatreds, as the press is want to do, but the negotiators understood full well, as did the European countries, the situation in the -- in the Balkans. This is not the first time in European history that the Balkans have been a difficult problem for the rest of Europe, as we all know. The second point is correct. The loss of Yugoslav strategic importance after the Cold War because Yugoslavia, having stood up to the Soviet Union, leader of the non-alined, did have greater significance during the Cold War period. The third point the difference of nationalism over democracy. Well, that's a rather cliched point; nobody would argue with that. A wavering decision of the Bush government; that's not correct. The Bush government did not waver. Five, the United States decision to transfer this issue to Europe instead of to NATO, that's also incorrect. And eventually a rather confused and rather passive European reply. That is largely correct. The European reply was not passive but one could not call it active, particularly in the military area. President Clinton's sixth factor about having a Muslim state in the heart of Europe, there were some individual European leaders who had that view, no doubt, but it has to be remembered that Albania was a -- a Muslim state in, as Clinton puts it, the heart of Europe. Albania was a member of the organisation of the Islamic conference, in fact. So there -- there was already a Muslim state in the Balkans, and Clinton is exaggerating this point. That's my answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. But would you agree with me if I said that he significantly contributed to creating the policies in the Balkans later on, to the way in which Bosnia-Herzegovina was in fact constructed? America and Bill Clinton had a significant contribution to make through the Washington Agreement and the Dayton agreement to the creation of Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we now see 3D 00858 on the screen, 3D 00858. It's in e-court. It's an interview with the general, Jacques Klein. You know who Mr. Jacques Klein was?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was not a general by the way. He was a career Foreign Service Officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, I'd just like to read out a brief passage. Towards the end of his interview Mr. Klein says the following: "There's a reality in politics that many people do not understand or do not want to see. They've told me this very same thing object numerous occasions," and he has Mr. Izetbegovic and Mr. Tudjman in mind. "I would act as you have suggested, Mr. Klein, but if I tell that to my people I shall lose their support. No, "Then he continues to say, "after Mr. Izetbegovic had indeed offered him the separation of Herzegovina, I openly asked the president of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Sarajevo about this issue, and he told me that the Croats were a major problem for him and that he want the to get rid of them, so he thought this was the best way. However, Tudjman did not accept the offer." And my question is as follows: In the course of your work, did you ever hear anything about Mr. Izetbegovic offering such a solution to Mr. Tudjman to have Herzegovina secede from Bosnia and Herzegovina and join Croatia and that Franjo Tudjman rejected this proposal?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never heard anything to that effect. Quite the contrary. Izetbegovic, Alija Izetbegovic, president of Bosnia, was adamant in public and private about maintaining the territorial integrity of the state. It was one of his idees fixes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll now mention five or six place names in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Trusina, Grabo -- Grabovica, Uzdol, Doljani, Hoducko, Gracanica, Krizancevo Selo. I'll stop there. Ambassador, my question is: Did you ever hear anything about these places I have just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: About Gracanica, yes, General. The others I don't recall. Excuse me, I should say Uzdol. Gracanica and Uzdol.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell me, why is it that you remember Uzdol and Gracanica?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was fighting there that apparently was heavy enough so that it was brought to our attention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd just like to remind you that on the 14th of September, 1993, a crime against the Croatian population was committed in Uzdol, and some ABiH units killed them. Twenty-one civilians were killed. Sixty-three in Doljani were killed. My question is as follows: If the television units weren't present, if they hadn't filmed what happened as they did in Stupni Do and Ahmici, then nothing in fact was known about the events. So this was an old thesis from communication theory; current communication theory, if it wasn't on the BBC or the CNN, it doesn't exist. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't agree with you, General, because we had UNPROFOR UN soldiers on the ground who investigated, and ECMM monitors. And you've just asked a question, and after 14 years I remembered Uzdol. So I think you can see that it was brought to our attention, because I can assure you in the intervening 14 years, from 1993 to April 2007, this is the first time I have heard Uzdol mentioned. I'm not objecting to that at all, but I do want to correct the -- your interpretation that it was not brought to our attention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. In any case, we can say that out of the names that I've mentioned you remembered two by the fighting that took place there, but you didn't tell me that you heard about the crimes that were committed against Croats over there. Yesterday, to my question --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, General. Thank you. When I talked about the fighting, I was subsuming the events of the killings. So we were aware of that also.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, did you know that Trusina is the place where 23 civilians, Croat civilians, were killed and that this happened on the same day, on the 16th when the crimes in Ahmici happened? However, you knew about Ahmici, but you didn't know about Trusina, irrespective of the European Monitors and other people. Please be honest and tell us, did you hear about Trusina at the same time you heard about Ahmici? And Trusina, I repeat, is the place where civilian Croats were killed, but this was not widely reported. Did you know about that event?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have reported, we were informed adequately and promptly, perhaps not always on the same day, but we were informed adequately and promptly by the European Community Monitoring Mission and by the UNPROFOR UN troops of events in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I cannot help wondering where you are going with your questions. I must confess that so far this morning I haven't heard anything that -- that I see how it could assist the Chamber. This Mr. Klein is hearsay five times removed, and it has -- I wonder what you are using the time for. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Trechsel, let me put it simply. I'm just trying to show the conflicts that existed within the international community with regard to the solutions to the problem. Second of all, Jacques Klein was not just anybody. He was the commissioner of the United Nations for the peaceful reintegration of Eastern Slavonia, and we can receive the statement from him, the one that we are reading from here. And as far as the TV reporting is concerned, unfortunately I cannot elaborate on that. But I just wanted to show that the opinions that were going on differed and were basically shaped in the light of the fact whether BBC was on the spot or not. And from such reporting, and it's very difficult to look at the burnt bodies, a conclusion was arrived at as to what was going on in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is just one topic that I cannot elaborate here with the ambassador, but I have very clear positions about what was going on and base on what information the positions arose, including the positions of the ambassador present here today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And my last question for the ambassador: Sir, yesterday when I asked you to give me an example from history, you mentioned the Japanese helping two sides in the Chinese civil war, but can you assume what the position of an army commander is when he's helping an army that would tomorrow use the same weapons that he helped them obtain and turn them against his own people? If we let convoys pass through, and we did it regularly, and the 250.000 soldiers that received those weapons turn those weapons against us on the following day, can you put yourself in the position of such a commander? And my question is this: Do you perhaps wonder how come that nobody actually killed me, assassinated me, knowing that I had led the weapons through and those same weapons were used to kill their brothers, fathers, and sisters? That's my last question, and could you please answer that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Before we do, Ambassador, my apology for interrupting you. Could we have the date of the convoy that Mr. Praljak is referring to, the particular convoy that he says those weapons were then used to kill Croatian soldiers? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] We have presented a series of documents about that, but I will remind Mr. Scott that I will present to the Trial Chamber a hundred thousand pages on CDs and 33 binders testifying to the help of the Republic of Croatia to the BiH army. So, Mr. Scott, you can expect a hundred thousand pages of documents in these proceedings to testify to the fact that during the course of the war between Muslims and Croats the weapons did not stop arriving. If you think logically, you can ask yourself: What weapons department the Muslims use if not the weapons that was let go through by the Croats all this time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, Mr. Scott asked you a question. He asked for a date. Your reply does not at all address this question. You speak about different things. It would be helpful if we were a bit more concentrated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I -- I don't think that my learned friend has the right to put questions to the accused. He can attempt to do that, but I don't think that the accused must answer him. Second of all, since I am on my feet, without any dates or numbers, so far we have introduced at least six documents that are clear evidence that from Croatia, in the course of 1992 and 1993, after the Croat and Muslim conflicts had already started, convoys carrying weapons would go through Croatia and -- and -- with the BH army. We have these exhibits in evidence, and I believe that Mr. Praljak's question is well-founded. In addition to that, the Defence has the right to anticipate the future evidence that they will introduce, and we will. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And another question, the ambassador testified yesterday that Croatia --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me. Before the question is put I want to respond to what has been said in response to the points I made. First of all, my question wasn't directed, of course, directly to Mr. Praljak; all I can do is object and ask for the Trial Chamber's assistance. So I'm not engaging in any dialogue with Mr. Praljak now or at any time, but I'm asking -- I did object to the question. I asked for the Court's intervention to sustain my objection and that that -- directs that information be directed to provide, number one. Number two, the reasons it's particularly relevant Your Honour, and we've addressed this before and I'm going to continue to address it whenever it's raised in this manner is, the Chamber is well advised by this point in the trial that in the course of the -- in the course of the war from 1991 to 1995 there were any number of places where indeed the Croats and the Muslims were fighting together against the Serbs, both in 1991 and 1992, again in 1994 and 1995, and indeed in some places even in 1993 while they were fighting each other they were also fighting together against the Serbs in various parts of Bosnia. So when these general statements are made about how we were arming the Muslims and sending them arms, it's -- it's only meaningful, only meaningful if it's very specific as to dates and locations because the fact that the -- Croatia provided arms to Bosnia in 1991 or early 1992 to fight the Serbs has no bearing on the point that Mr. Praljak is trying to make about assisting them in killing their own soldiers. I asked a very specific -- my objection was very specific -- excuse me. My objection was very specific, and Mr. Praljak chose to frame his question by referring to a date and a particular convoy that he said he was on and that those weapons were used the next day to kill HVO soldiers. That's my objection. I want him to tell me the date and so the ambassador can properly frame his answer specifically to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Praljak, the Prosecutor has raised an objection. He told you a few minutes ago that he doesn't contest the fact that weapons were provided in 1991 and in 1992, but when it comes to the crucial period, the relevant period, which is 1993, if you believe that the question that you are putting to the witness also refers to 1993, could you pinpoint the period that you're referring to when you're talking about the weapons that were sent or provided to BiH army? I believe that I remember having seen documents that talk about the delivery of arms. I don't have these documents before me. You certainly know these documents better than I do, and I believe that you are better suited than me to remember the dates of these documents. Mr. Praljak, could you please be more precise and rephrase your question by introducing a precise date into your question, because this is the gist of the Prosecutor's objection to your question. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, not only five or six but over 20 or even 30 documents have been presented to the Trial Chamber referring to the period up to April 1993 and even later. Actually, the 4th of October, 1993, talking about Arif Pasalic. There was a witness here, and I'm not going to mention his name, who said it clearly that the arms arrived in Mostar in the summer of 1993. In Mr. Okun's diary, the same thing -- the same thing is mentioned. Fourth of all, the ambassador when I asked him yesterday also confirmed to me that weapons did arrive from Croatia and through Croatia and ended up with the BH army in the course of the entire war. My question is only logical and well-founded. At this moment I don't have any documents, and I'm kindly asking the ambassador to answer my question in any way he can or will.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, do you know that through Croatia from Turkey, from Iran, from Argentina, from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak -- THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- weapons arrived --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You put this question yesterday and it is answered. It is answered, this question, and we really do not have the time to have the same question put twice to the same witness. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Very well then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Okun, if you can provide your opinion, I would be grateful to you, to the Trial Chamber. Ambassador, thank you very much for having answered my questions, and I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we now go to the other Defence team. Ms. Alaburic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ambassador, good day to you. I represent General Milivoj Petkovic in these proceedings, and I would like to clarify a few things with you because I believe that your rich diplomatic experience, the experience as a political analyst can help the Trial Chamber to understand the events in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. I have just provided you with a binder of documents that I will be using during the course of this cross-examination, but this will obviously depend on your answers to my questions. In your diary you mentioned Badinter Commission, and yesterday on several occasions you commenced this commission before this Trial Chamber. And that is why my question to you is this: Is this the commission that was composed of legal experts of five European countries that were supposed to define the legal rules for, as you've said it, a peaceful separation or divorce of the republics of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Badinter Commission, whose name was actually the Commission d'Arbitrage, the chairman was the very distinguished French former Minister of Justice, now Senator Robert Badinter, was designed to answer -- I should say was asked many questions by Lord Carrington in order to it assist the conference on Yugoslavia, which Lord Carrington headed, across the broad range of issues. One of them of course was the separation, but there were other issues as well. The Badinter Commission was designed to answer -- to seek to answer from the legal point of view, from the point of view of public international law, the whole range of questions of a legal nature.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this very detailed answer. And now could you please look at a document in my binder. At the same time I would kindly ask for the document to be placed on e-court the number is 4D 00540. Those are three opinions provided by the Badinter Commission to the questions put to them by Lord Carrington. What I am interested in at the moment is the question of borders. Opinion number 2, which is on page 3 of this document, concerns the issue as to whether the Serbs in Croatia, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, as a constituent people within Yugoslavia, might be given the right to self-determination. That's under item 1. And it says here: "The commission is of the opinion that the right to self-determination must not involve changes to the existing frontiers at the time when the independence is gained, save for the situation in which the states concerned agree otherwise." Let's also look at the opinion number 3, which reference to the issue of internal borders between Serbia and Croatia, and between Bosnia and Herzegovina and Serbia, and whether these borders could be considered frontiers in terms it of the international public law. Under item 2 -- 2, Second, it says: "The boundaries between Croatia and Serbia and between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Serbia, may not be altered except by agreement freely arrived at by the parties." I am interpreting from the English original. That is why there may be slight discrepancies between what you are receiving in your headphones and what you're reading on the screen. Ambassador, these opinions provide by the committee, did they become the positions of the conference for Yugoslavia and later on by the ministerial council of the European Union, and finally all the relevant factors on the European and international political scene?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these positions, these opinions rendered by the Commission d'Arbitrage were widely accepted by the international community.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Okun, you're probably familiar with the fact that the ministerial council of the European Union, on the 16th of December, 1991, in Brussels passed directions for the recognition of new states in east Europe and the former Soviet Union, or guidelines for the recognition of those newly emerged states.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's partially correct, but in addition to that, Ms. Alaburic, the EC and Lord Carrington's conference on Yugoslavia formally requested that the Badinter Commission pass on -- make a judgement on whether the four republics that had declared independence were eligible for recognition by the European Commission. The four republics, of course, were Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Macedonia. Those were the four republics that in December 1991 had already declared their independence. They had not been recognised by anybody, and Lord Carrington asked the Badinter Commission to render an opinion as to whether and which republics merited recognition.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What you have just told us does not refer directly to the document that I've asked you about, but I am familiar with what you have just mentioned, and there's no contest about that. But let's look at a document that I was asking you about. Let's look at 4D 00542. All these documents are in a sequence and arise from what you have been telling us. In this document the guidelines for the recognition of new states in east Europe and the Soviet Union, which were adopted on the 16th of December, 1991. What I'm interested in are just boundaries. If we can look together the third bullet where it says that the joint position is adopted in the process of the recognition of new states, which requires, under bullet three, "respect for the inviolability of all frontiers which can only be changed by peaceful means and by common agreement." I suppose you're familiar with this document, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's perfectly standard. After all, it's in the United Nations charter that you don't change boundaries by force; it's in the League of Nation charter. This is hardly a great discovery on December 16th, 1941 [sic]. It's standard practice. I mean, it's only understood one does not change international boundaries by force otherwise it's aggression as defined in Article 2 of the United Nations Charter.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Okun, at this moment we're talking about 1991 and Yugoslavia. At that time there were still no internationally recognised boundaries. We are talking about something that up to then was considered internal boundaries of the republics within the state that was known as Yugoslavia. So this is not rephrasing international laws but this had a huge bearing on the future organisation of the former republics of Yugoslavia. Wouldn't you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I already answered in a question yesterday, the EC in accordance with the Helsinki agreement of 1975 had already decided that the internal boundaries in the former Yugoslavia could not be altered except by mutual agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All these documents preceded that final position in a way, but I believe that we can agree that the international community would not recognise any alterations of the boundaries of the republics of the former Yugoslavia unless they agreed it upon those alterations in a peaceful way. Wasn't that the position that was the starting point for the conference on the former Yugoslavia and every other institution after that that dealt with the issue of the former Yugoslavia? Wouldn't you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I suppose that we will also agree that these decisions, as well as all the other decisions supplied by the international institutions were something that the Croatian President, Franjo Tudjman, was familiar with? Do you know that for a fact? Was he familiar with all these decisions that were passed concerning the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't speak for the president on every single issue, but on the broad question of whether Croatia's borders, for example, with the internal borders of Yugoslavia, whether they were all of Croatia and could not be changed, yes, he certainly was familiar with that. It came up indeed very importantly in our negotiations, that is Secretary Vance and me, our negotiations for the cessation of hostilities in Croatia during the -- during the Serbian invasion of Croatia. So it was definitely on his mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, could President Tudjman consider that this applied only to Croatia or that that was the rule that was applicable to all the republics of the former Yugoslavia? What could have been his opinion until?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: His opinion that I was aware of was in the main concerned with Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that you didn't know that President Tudjman, when it came to the AVNOJ borders, whatever he might consider about them, was something that the international community would not change or would not allow to be changed unless there was an agreement between the parties that were interested in those borders? Does this mean that you didn't know that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it does not mean that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you know that Franjo Tudjman knew that this rule as worded in these documents was applicable to all the republics of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm quite confident the president knew it as an abstract fashion that did not necessarily affect his views as to the application of his policies and those of the Herceg-Bosna people within Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Okun, we will come to Herceg-Bosna a bit later. Now I would like to talk about the principles of the matter and clarify the starting points for our future communication. In your view and according to your knowledge, was President Tudjman aware that opening the issue of any alterations to the so-called AVNOJ borders of the republics of the former Yugoslavia would also open an issue of the alterations to the boundaries of Croatia, i.e., the separation of the area of the Republic of Croatia where Croats, Serbs, resided and where the so-called Krajina had been established?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I've said, he was very aware of the Croatian situation. The Serbs, as we will all know, tried both militarily and politically to detach Eastern Slavonia from Croatia. That was the area of the heaviest fighting indeed, so that he was surely aware of the need to protect Croatia's borders. And may I please give you one concrete example of President Tudjman's awareness of his -- I can't give it? I was answering your question. That's okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Okun, believe me, that I'm listening to your answer was a lot of interest, but I want to get through all of this with you, and unfortunately I have very little time. You mentioned Eastern Slavonia. Tell me, was there a problem relating to borders in the territory of western Slavonia and in the territory of the Knin Krajina which during that period of time was under the control of the Croatian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Western Slavonia was much less of a problem, although the Serbs in Croatia, as you know, had declared an autonomous region, a SAO, of Eastern Slavonia, western Slavonia, and the Krajina, but in western Slavonia it was not a problem because the Croatian armed forces drove the Serbs out of western Slavonia and the Croatian army was in control of western Slavonia by the end of 1991. The Krajina was a separate problem being 90 per cent populated by Serbs. It had a sort of de facto autonomy, but those were the areas that precisely for this reason the peacekeeping operation that Secretary Vance and I developed had four non-connected, non-contiguous protected areas, namely Eastern Slavonia, western Slavonia, and the north and south parts of the Krajina. This was to avoid and to make impossible the Serb, the Serb desire to draw a -- have a cease-fire along the line of confrontation which would have given to the Serbs one-fourth or so of Croatia, and we wouldn't -- President Tudjman would not agree with that, and we certainly did not agree with that. So for the first time in history a cessation of hostilities with the peacekeeping operations for them did not have a contiguous front line, sort of like a green line like they have in Cyrus, like you have in Israel in 1949. Finally, the Vance-Owen Plan naturally at President Tudjman's strong insistence -- excuse me, I didn't mean the Vance-Owen Plan. I'm talking about Vance Plan, the peacekeeping operations for Croatia required the withdrawal of JNA forces from all of Croatia. So we were attentive, and, to answer your question completely, President Tudjman was very attentive to the need to retain the territorial integrity and maintain it's territorial integrity of Croatia. I'm sorry for the long answer but one really must try to give the Chamber the full picture. I'm trying to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the last part of your answer you in fact said what I was going to ask you about, and that is that the main concern of President Tudjman at the time was to maintain the territorial integrity of the Republic of Croatia within the borders such as they were at the time of Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. That's why he demanded and we demanded the withdrawal of the JNA from all of Croatia. The immediate withdrawal, which the Serbs did not do but the JNA finally did leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Okun, according to your information, in order to obtain that objective did -- or, rather, was Mr. Tudjman one of the first persons to ask for international arbitration when it came to solving the problem of the break-up the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he was one of the first. There was a general desire from the European Community to establish an arbitration concerning the declarations of independence of Slavonia and Croatia. He certainly would have been in the advan [phoen], but there was a widespread desire very quickly, almost immediately after the June 25, 1991 declarations, the EC was in action. I do not say that to criticise President Tudjman; simply to point out that he was not alone.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Okun, I didn't even mean to imply that he was the only one, but I think it amounted to knocking on an open door, the open door of the international community in a certain sense, but I wanted to say that he was one of the first individuals from the territory of the former Yugoslavia who requested the arbitration of the international community. Could we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could we also agree that he was one of the first from the territory of the former Yugoslavia who requested that the UN peace forces be deployed in areas where there was ongoing combat in order to attempt to establish peace there?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true. Paradoxically enough, it was Milosevic who was the first to suggest it. That's in my diaries. It's quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Okun, I didn't say the first, but one of the first. So could we agree --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was a conflict between two parties. Milosevic was the first. He was the second. That means he was the last. You could also say he was one of the first, but there were only two parties, and if you're the second, you know, then that makes you the last. Now, I have to tell the Chamber, it must be said that Milosevic did not suggest this peacekeeping operation out of benevolence or goodwill towards President Tudjman. He wanted it to -- as I've just said, he wanted a green line. He wanted UN troops on the line of confrontation, which would have left the JNA controlling one-fourth to one-third of Croatia. That's why he suggested the peacekeeping operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Okun, could we agree that Mr. Milosevic's initiative concerned the occupied territory in Croatia, whereas Mr. Tudjman's initiative concerned the borders between the republics of the former Yugoslavia, which at the time already had the status of independent states?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, President Tudjman, as we said several times, was of course interested in retaining and maintaining the territorial integrity of Croatia. That's precisely why he would not accept the concept of the green line.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did Milosevic in fact want international peace forces to protect the Serbs in occupied areas in Croatia, whereas Mr. Tudjman wanted the state borders to be protected from the arrival of foreign enemy troops?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: President Tudjman wanted the JNA to withdraw entirely from Croatia so that Croatia would be master of its own destiny. He fully agreed to our concept of the four discontinuous UN-protected areas along with the full withdrawal of the JNA from Croatia. Yes, he was always concerned about the borders. Understandably so.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Okun, could you answer my question a little more precisely, my question as to whether Mr. Tudjman wanted international forces to be deployed at the borders of Croatia. So when the JNA had already left Croatia, he wanted international forces to protect the borders of the Croatian state. If you can't add any more detailed information to your answer, we can move on.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can answer that precisely, because it was a subject of very intense negotiations between Mr. Vance and me and President Tudjman and Milosevic. President Tudjman's initial position was that the JNA withdraw completely from Croatia, tout de suite, nothing else. Milosevic's position was, as I've said -- I have to answer your question. I'm sorry. I --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Okun, we don't have the time.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you asked the question and I'm trying to answer it as briefly, as accurately, but also as fully as I can, and if you wouldn't interrupt me, we would have been finished by now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Okun, I do apologise, and it's really not my intention to be rough or impolite, but we really can't go into the subject of the internal relationships and the situation in Croatia and the war in Croatia. I'm only interested in the subject of borders at this point in time, and perhaps we could focus on the borders. As to this request for the JNA to withdraw from Croatia, I think we have dealt with that and you have provided us with a detailed explanation about that matter. I would just like to now establish that Mr. Tudjman wanted the international forces to be deployed at the borders of the Republic of Croatia. That is important for me so that I can continue to analyse the relationship with neighbouring Bosnia and Herzegovina had, and that's why I'm trying to restrict myself to the issue of borders, but personally I'd be extremely interested in the situation in Croatia and in the events that transpired there. I do apologise and it really is not my intention to be impolite. Perhaps we can move on. In your opinion, was President Tudjman a realistic and pragmatic politician?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And tell me, like other politicians, did he sometimes express certain positions in order to see what the position of the other party was with regard to a certain issue?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not his style. President Tudjman was a very serious man. As I responded and as Mr. Karnavas read the interview I gave correctly about President Tudjman, you will recall I said he was in style rather rigid. He was not a person to play around with ideas. So the answer to that question is basically no.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, according to your information did President Tudjman always express his opinion about certain issues in public and quite openly or in order to find out what his position was about certain issues did you have to engage the services of certain secret services, and did you have to tap into secret sources of information?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not in the hands of the secret services, Mr. Vance and I, and Lord Owen, when he joined us, spoke frequently with President Tudjman. We were aware, of course, of his public statements, and we took them into account. Naturally we paid the most attention to what he told us privately. I think you can understand that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you have any information about the position President Tudjman held with regard to Bosnia-Herzegovina, and would you say that this is a position that you didn't hear about from him directly or position that you didn't read about in the media or in some book?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We heard about it directly from President Tudjman, and then, of course, we could see it in his meetings with Izetbegovic, for example. He disliked Izetbegovic intensely. He said that to us. He told it to Izetbegovic, in effect to his face. He always referred to Izetbegovic, to us, as "the fundamentalist." The fundamentalist Izetbegovic. With respect to Izetbegovic's governance of the state, he was scornful and scoffed at it and maintain that Izetbegovic would not even be in power were it not for the Croats defending him. He did not respect Izetbegovic, nor Izetbegovic's governance of the state. He made that quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Ambassador, could we agree that President Tudjman publicly spoke about the fact that the AVNOJ Croatian borders were, in his opinion, unjust?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The AVNOJ borders? I don't recall he made too much of it. There were times -- actually, I don't want to go into it, but it was the -- it was the Serbs who complained more about the AVNOJ borders. They complained so much that I had a direct discussion with Milovan Djilas [Realtime transcript read in error "Gilos"] in December 1991, because Djilas was the person who was in charge for Tito in 1945 of deciding on the borders, and the Serbs were so violently opposed to it in their style than I immediately contacted Milovan Djilas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: For the record would you like to spell out the name because here it is written with a G.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's D-j-i-l-a-s. D as in David, J as in jota, I as in item, L as in Lawrence, A as in able, S as in sugar. Djilas, Milovan Djilas.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: On the basis of your answer could I correctly draw the conclusion that President Tudjman believed the existing borders of Croatia to be just? And I'd like to point out that the existing borders means the AVNOJ borders.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he never went that far because he, as a military man, and I've mentioned this in previous testimony, was very aware of the Cazinska Krajina and its strategic importance to Croatia. He pointed out to me frequently that the main railway between Belgrade and the major cities of the Dalmatian coast cut through Bosnia-Herzegovina, went through the Cazinska Krajina. He was also very aware, needless to say, of the Serbs in the -- in -- who lived in Croatia and who straddled the border, the Krajina being heavily occupied, on both sides of the border, that is to say the Croatian side and the Bosnian side, with the Serb self-declared capital of Knin. That was a concern to him. And he was well aware and often said that Croatia -- just in passing that this Croatia, the AVNOJ borders, was but a shadow of its former self.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Okun, could we now try to define President Tudjman's attitude towards the Croatian borders? Was he content with those borders or not? You answered negatively to both those questions, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think he envisaged an enlargement, either directly or via Herceg-Bosna joining into Croatia at some day. I've said that in my witness statement, and I've been repeatedly asked questions by everybody, and I think that I've answered it adequately. I'm happy to answer it again.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: No, you don't have to answer that question again, but I would now like to briefly discuss wishes and reality. What someone wants in politics and the possibilities he sees of obtaining such objectives. Do you know who Josip Manolic is? Are you familiar with that name? Josip Manolic.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of that name?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not familiar with that name. I've seen it, but I really am not familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I wanted to quote him, as I believed that you would know who this person was, but I'll paraphrase what he said. He was a witness in this case. In 1992 and 1993 he was one of President Tudjman's closest associates. He was involved in a political conflict with Gojko Susak, and in 1994 he left the Croatian Democratic Union, the HDZ. He said here that Franjo Tudjman was a very realistic politician who would never gamble, and I paraphrase. He would never gamble with the fate of Croatia. He would never put the fate of Croatia on the line in order to obtain some of his objectives. And one of his wishes concerned the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina where the Croatian population was in the majority. Mr. Okun, since you yourself have described Franjo Tudjman as a realistic and pragmatic politician, would he ever endanger the fate of Croatia in order to obtain a small parcel of the territory of some other state?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In supporting Mate Boban and the Herceg-Bosna people, he was in no way endangering Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: As far as supporting Mate Boban and Herceg-Bosna is concerned, this very same gentleman, Mr. Manolic, said that Croatia was involved in pursuing the following policies, and I will now quote him. He said, page 4319 of the transcript that the policies pursued by Tudjman with regard to Herceg-Bosna was as follows -- Mr. Okun, I haven't shown you this document. It's not among the bundle of documents. This is not an exhibit, but I will quote from it and I will read it out in English to make sure what I say is not misinterpreted. [In English] "He upheld the position that I too upheld. Organise yourself, mobilise yourself in your environments where you feel in jeopardy and stand up to the aggression, and we will help you within the frameworks and possibilities that we are allowed to do because we are also threatened by the same aggressor." [Interpretation] Would you agree with this statement made by someone who left Franjo Tudjman in 1994 for political reasons?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's clear -- it's clear that President Tudjman here is talking about resisting the Serbs. He uses the term "aggressor," but it's understandable, and he says we are all -- we are threatened by the Serbs. True. Even though the cease-fire existed there were obviously problems with Serbian bad faith. And you, too, in Bosnia, we want to oppose the Serbs. So that's completely consistent, and I've -- indeed I've so stated in my witness statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Okun, in order to conclude, I have one more question before the break. Could we agree that Franjo Tudjman, being a realistic and pragmatic politician, would never have attempted to use force and to ignore the desires of the international community in order to change the borders of his state, because he was aware of the fact that, first of all, it wasn't possible for him to do this; and secondly, if he had made such an attempt this long waited state would have covered very serious consequences and would have been seriously harmed?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: President Tudjman's realism and pragmatism was also tempered by a very strong sense of Croatian history. He was perhaps unique among the -- all of the Yugoslav -- former Yugoslav leaders in his deep understanding so that his fight against Serbian and JNA aggression in Croatia and his desire for an independent state of Herceg-Bosna via Mate Boban and his people were actually quite consistent, and he made that clear to us. There was no doubt about it. I've so stated in my witness statement. He made it clear to us that he supported the goals, aims, activities of Mate and his people.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Okun.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll have a 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll now resume.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, before I continue with my cross-examination I'd like to ask you something about the time we have at our disposal. In the meantime, we have had consultations with our client, and I believe that half an hour for procedural matters would be quite sufficient, so I would like to know whether it might be possible to be granted additional time for the cross-examination of Witness Okun, if you believe that the questions might be relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber has granted the Defence teams eight hours. So far five hours and 40 minutes have been used up, but the registrar will make any corrections if necessary. Eight hours and less five hours and 40 minutes, well, that is the time that the Defence has at its disposal.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Okun, in response to my last question, you said something that we cannot find in your statement, and it's also something that can't be found in your diary if I didn't miss it, and no one has said such a thing in this courtroom, and I, who was a relatively well-informed citizen of the Republic of Croatia, am also not aware of any such thing. The desire of President Tudjman was apparently to establish the independent state of Herceg-Bosna. For the sake of the transcript, let me clarify this. Let me clarify the last sentence with regard to the desire of Mr. Tudjman. This was a quote from Mr. Okun's answer to my last question. It can be found in line 35 [as interpreted] of today's transcript.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me a question?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: My question is: Can you tell us where this can be found in your statement or in your diary, where we can find the statement that President Tudjman's desire was to create the independent state of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that President Tudjman supported the goals, aim, and actions of the -- of Mate Boban and his people. Those were my words. I refer you, counsel, to paragraph 6 of my witness statement where, after I give the war aims, and I'll just repeat the last war aim, "to erect and maintain" -- I'm quoting from paragraph 6 of my witness statement: "To erect and maintain a separate Bosnian Croat entity (Herceg-Bosna) which could eventually unite with the Republic of Croatia formally or informally. These war aims were made clear to the international negotiators throughout the 1992/1993 period by the Bosnian Croat leadership, Mate Boban and his associates. President Tudjman privately gave the negotiators to understand that he fully supported these aims." That is the end of paragraph 6 of my witness statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Okun, in item 6 of your statement -- well, this is identical to all the statements of Mate Boban that you noted in your diary, and they relate to the creation of a Croatian entity within Bosnia and Herzegovina. So within the borders of an international -- of the internationally recognised state of Bosnia-Herzegovina. If this is not the case, can you tell me where we can find a different statement given by Mate Boban in your diary or of any other representative of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We've discussed this extensively, Counsel, in this Chamber. Both the Bosnian Serbs, Radovic -- Karadzic and others, and the Bosnian Croats knew that at the initial phase they would have to remain within the borders of the Bosnian state. Their aims, however, went beyond that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So when we're talking about the creation of a Croatian entity in Bosnia and Herzegovina, can we claim for certain that we're always talking about the internal organisation of an independent and sovereign state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that all the negotiations about the internal structure of the state, and this includes the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, in fact concerned such an organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina as an independent state?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Vance-Owen Peace Plan, like all the other peace plans, envisaged a sovereign, independent Bosnian state. You will recall that in the constitutional principles of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan it was explicitly forbidden for any of the provinces to have relations with any foreign state or international organisation. That was inserted in the constitutional provisions of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan precisely to obviate what we knew to be the Bosnian Serb and the Bosnian Croat goal, to have special relations with their mother countries. Otherwise, there would have been no need for that constitutional provision. I don't know how I can answer that any more clearly than that, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, given the Dayton agreement and the rules in Bosnia-Herzegovina, was it possible to have close ties of the entities of neighbouring countries? For example, between the Republika Srpska and the former Yugoslavia or what is now Serbia?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the Dayton agreement?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, in accordance with the Dayton agreement and the regulations in force in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina at this time?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Dayton agreement of November 19 --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This is quite sufficient.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: It's sufficient for you to say yes?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not sufficient, Counsel. I'm very sorry, it's not. The Dayton --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Okun, either the regulations allow for this or they don't. Therefore, at this moment all that is important for me is to have a yes or no answer, because, believe me, I don't have enough time for any other details.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I sympathise with you. If you wish to silence me, so be it. The floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Naturally I don't wish to silence you. You are here not to remain silent, but I would appreciate it if you could answer my questions by saying yes or no, and if you say this is not possible, then I will decide to ask you for further explanations or whether to move on to another subject. If I have understood you correctly, it's not possible to answer this question with a yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will answer it: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. On the 3rd of April, page 10, you said that the Vance-Owen Peace Plan was very generous when it came to maps, but it was just in relation to the Croats. Do you remember that statement of yours?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what you meant by generosity? Why was it generous?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was generous because in the mixed Bosnian Croat, Bosnian Muslim areas the benefit of the doubt was given by and large to the Bosnian Croats, and that is why Izetbegovic refused to sign the map, and that was evident from the day the map was officially presented on January 1993. Indeed, I was told -- I wasn't in Zagreb at the time, but I was told that there were newspaper headlines that said HVO stood for "Hvala Vance-Owen," "thank you Vance-Owen," and they were referring to the map. I have since learned that indeed there were statements and headlines to that effect so that the Bosnian Croats, as well as the Croatian people, were very satisfied with their treatment, the provincial boundaries established by the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. Have I answered your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much. Can we focus on more -- on certain provinces to see what this exactly would mean there? Can we be more concrete therefore? I assume you have this map, and let's have a look at the map. In which provinces would the Vance-Owen Plan be generous? According to those criteria, which provinces would be considered as provinces in which Croats were in the majority or in which provinces would the Croats have benefited from this generosity? Could you provide us with an interpretation?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A glance at the map indicates, if we look at province number 8, you will note that the eastern side, the central eastern side, is completely green, meaning it's completely Muslim, and next to it is a blue, large blue area where the Serbs are, and there are scattered Muslim areas throughout 8, but you -- it would have been very easy to draw the line straight, you know, and put -- put all of that green area into a -- into province 7, a Muslim-majority province. Likewise, province 10 at the very northern tip, you see a point there that's all green and was Muslim included in a Croat-majority province. And 9 is half and half. So there's no question that the Vance-Owen map was thoroughly more than -- more than acceptable, generous to the Bosnian Croats. Now, I must add at this point that the provinces were not to be ethnically based - that was the essence of Vance-Owen - so that they tried very hard to make sure that there were balances in -- in the provinces in order to emphasise the multi-ethnic character of the country. And I've given you yesterday -- I won't repeated today, but I've stated yesterday the numbers of percentages of Croats, Muslims, and Serbs who were outside of their majority provinces. That was bitterly opposed, particularly by the Bosnian Serbs. Their lawyer Buha used to say to us, "You've given the Croats and the Muslims everything. All we Serbs got were the rattlesnakes and the stones of Western Bosnia." So one has to take that into consideration. But there's no question that the Bosnian Croats were well-treated in this plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Alaburic, perhaps you wanted to put the same thing, but may I just take up a small point? Ambassador, you have referred to the province number 9, but that, if I understand correctly -- I see -- I leave it to you, Ms. Alaburic. You wanted to ask the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We wanted -- I wanted to clear up the question of province number 9, of which you said it was half-half. But I see in province 9 very little areas inhabited by Croats. So did you really mean half-half, half Muslims and half Croats, or did you have in mind a different ratio?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said half-half -- excuse me, I said it rarely loosely, just to mean that there were people there. Sorry, I apologise to the Chamber for the imprecision in my remarks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: My point was slightly different. You started off speaking of the "Croat provinces," and in these -- in this framework you mentioned 9, which according to the map that I have in front of me is green.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was my error, Judge. That's what I just apologised for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Okun, we shall now go back to the issue of multi-ethnicity. I am aware that in addition to ethnicity you had in mind many other criteria in the formation of the provinces. Therefore, if I have noted correctly, the 29 per cent of Croats that would remain outside the provinces with the Croatian relative majority; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Are we talking about 29 per cent Croats -- of Croats remaining outside provinces 3, 8, and 10?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would be the number. It would be the number remaining outside provinces 3, 8, and 10. You're entirely correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now let me focus on my client. So will you, in my set of documents, look at an interview given by Milivoj Petkovic in February 1993, number 4D 00100. Could we please look at the final passages of that interview. That is the last page of it. I will be concentrating on the answer to the last question and the last part of the answer to the previous question. Speaking about the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, General Petkovic says, and I quote: "For us representatives of the Croatian people were most interested in the first and seventh part of the Geneva document. In the first there is reference to the cessation of hostilities, and the seventh said that within a period of 45 days all units in Herceg-Bosna must retreat to their provinces." Have you managed to find that last part of the interview, the last page?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm looking for it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm reading it as it is written.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe you, but I can't find it. Perhaps somebody could help me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: It is the last -- fifth page?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel approach the microphone, please, and speak up a little.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If I could just show like this. This is the third passage from above.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have found it, counsel. We, the representatives, the Croatian people. That's what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This seventh section of the Geneva document which speaks of the retreat of military units to their provinces within a period of 45 days, can you explain what this really entails? I will assist you by telling you where exactly it can be found in the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, the document shown to you by the Prosecution, P 9852.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. I know quite well where it is in the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. Thank you for your assistance, but it's not necessary. The Vance-Owen Peace Plan --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let me say this for the benefit of those who don't find their way as easily. It's Annex VII, page 36 of the Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I answer the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There are two relevant portions in the Vance-Owen Peace Plan to the question you've raised. The first is section E of the first annex to the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, as printed by the United Nations. The identifying number is S, as in Samuel, /25479, page 12, and I will quote, it's very brief, what it says about withdrawal of forces. This is the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. "Sarajevo province shall be immediately demilitarised. All Serb forces shall withdraw into provinces 2, 4, and 6; HVO forces into province 3; Bosnian army forces into province 1. Both Bosnian army and HVO forces shall be deployed in provinces 5, 8, 9, and 10. Under arrangements agreed between them the process of demilitarisation shall apply to it all forces in these nine provinces," and then it goes on to say how it should be carried out. Then in annex VIII of the plan, on page 41 of the same UN document, it reads: "To enable the process of return to normalcy and as a direct follow-on for the cessation of hostilities and the separation of forces," and here I interject, "the separation of forces," of course, is the passage that I've just read to you where the provinces -- where they go. To continue reading, "And the separation of forces and a return to the designated provinces will be conducted." So you have this paragraph that you read that states the general principles, that the separation of forces and they will go to provinces, and then you have the complete section, section E, about the disposition of the forces inside the provinces, and it's really quite clear. Now, when General Petkovic was making this interview, which I'm seeing for the first time today but that's fine, when he was giving this interview I see the date is sometime in February 1993. Am I correct? It says Vecernji List, date: 16 February. So this was already one month after the Bosnian Croat defence minister had issued what was an illegal order, really, because it was inconsistent with the Vance Plan about the subordination of HVO units in certain provinces to the HV -- excuse me, the subordination of Bosnian army units to the HVO and of other provinces. That was not in line at all with the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. We've discussed that, I know, but I think since you raise it again I have to make clear that when General Petkovic says what they were interested in, and he says it rather incompletely, to put it mildly -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I apologise --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I appreciate --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: -- Mr. Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope I've answered your question. I do just try to speak for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I will come to my client's order that of you have just mentioned, but let us do that in the way I think is best. At the beginning of your answer, you say -- you talk about a section A of the first annex, and you talk about the return of Serb forces to provinces 2, 4, and 6, of the Croatian forces to 1, and then the agreement between the army and the HVO to provinces 5, 8, 9, and 10, and you're referring to the introductory statement by Lord Owen. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at page 12 that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 12 is the document itself. It's not an introductory statement. It is the -- it is the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. I mean, there's no question about that. I don't know -- I don't know -- I can't imagine what you're referring to when you call it a statement by Lord Owen. It's the text of the peace plan. It's Annex I, agreement on interim arrangements, capital A, interim Presidency and interim government. Capital B -- let me finish, please. Let me finish, please. Boundary commission. Capital C, Sarajevo; capital D, provinces; capital E, withdrawal of forces. It has nothing to do with the statement of Lord Owen. It's the text of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Okun, for the record I wanted to indicate this, and that in the document P 09052 that I was referring to, on pages 11, 12, and 13, is the introductory statement by Lord Owen, and I wouldn't dwell on that any more because of the shortage of time.
