I should like us to look into the order of my client, which you haven't seen yet in this courtroom. You have only seen the order by Mr. Prlic. Now, will you look at my set of documents, please. Document number P 01135. It is an order by General Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We an agree from the introduction that it refers to the order of the head of the defence department, dated the 15th of January. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's -- that's what it says, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This is an order that my colleagues from Mr. Stojic's Defence will be discussing, but I will focus only on the part that differs from the order of Mr. Prlic. The decision of the Croatian Defence Council signed by the president of the HVO, Dr. Jadranko Prlic. Paragraph number 5 of this order, of General Petkovic's order, says: "Use forces of the Central Bosnia operative zone to close all routes from the area of Zenica towards the area under the control of the -- this zone." This is the implementation of the agreement. Mr. Okun, in January 1993, were you familiar with the directive of the commander of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel speak up, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Counsel, before I answer, could I ask you a question? I didn't understand something you just said. May I ask a question? The quotation is: "This is the implementation of the agreement," and I don't understand what implementation you're talking about or what agreement you're talking about. Could you expand on that, please? What implementation? What agreement?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In the introduction it says: "Pursuant to agreements on the regulation of Bosnia and Herzegovina." So the entire order relates to the annex that we were looking at a moment ago about the withdrawal of military units to provinces within a delay of 45 days. And this agreement on Joint Commands, if that is what you're referring to, did you know that there were any agreements between the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of any agreements.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us look at the document 4D 00395. It's a document from November 1992, signed by the Chief of Staff of the Main Staff of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Sefer Halilovic. And could we look through this document together quickly. In the introduction paragraph 2, second sentence says: "During discussions about joint commands, it is necessary to make arrangements which, for example, in the Mostar Corps the appointed commanding officer selected from the HVO, and the person from the Bosnian army and so forth in terms of percentage based on the actual number of soldiers for all headquarters and units on the territory under the responsibility of the Mostar Corps. For Zenica the person in command should be appointed from the BH army, and the other person from the HVO units. This should be the principle applied also for appointing commanding officers of the smallest army units up to the headquarters. You, when reaching agreement, you can refer to an agreement reached between President Izetbegovic and Mr. Mate Boban." Has this document refreshed your memory about information about the formation of joint commands?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It refreshes my memory. The document refreshes my memory of the sequence of events, yes. Early November, immediately followed the HVO depredation in Prozor, so there was a period of intense activity. It wasn't the first and it wasn't the last, but there was a period of intense activity to try and bring the HVO and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina into a better relationship. It did not work, and again we had heavy activity as you know and we discussed in January and again in April of 1993. So this statement concerns the situation post-Prozor in October, November 1992. The document which you displayed for the Chamber, General Petkovic's order of 16 February 1993, referred to a quite different situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you clarify something with regard to the 16th of February, 1993? You have the interview in mind, do you?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have in mind the document that you showed us.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Interview.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Okun --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was actually referring to the order, not the interview. But they are roughly congruent.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The order I am referring to was issued on the 15th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the date of the order you showed me. The interview was 16 February. My point in answering was to make clear to you that that followed the introduction of the Vance-Owen Plan with section E concerning the disposition and redeployment of -- of orders. Excuse me. I said, "redeployment of orders." Could that please be changed to redeployment of forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Okun, are you aware of the fact that these decisions or orders dated the 15th of January, and when I use the plural I'm also referring to the HVO decision and to the Ministry of Defence and the chief of the Main Staff, are you aware of the fact that those decisions were also provided to members of the ABiH or, rather, to Bosnia and Herzegovina, representatives of Bosnia and Herzegovina? And this proposal was discussed, and in fact the other side rejected this proposal.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We have had that introduced in the Chamber, President Izetbegovic's denunciation of the order issued by the defence minister, which as we all recall he said was unilateral and therefore illegal.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Just a minor clarification. It concerns the order from the minister of defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but I'm referring to the order of the minister of defence of Herceg-Bosna. In any event, what's important to me is that you have just said that you know that representatives of Bosnia-Herzegovina or, rather, representatives it of the ABiH rejected this proposal. And now for my following question. Are you aware of the fact that there was no obstacle to implementing these orders or, rather, the units of the ABiH were not disarmed, and no one insisted on having them resubordinated to certain units, nor did anyone insist on having them resubordinated to units that were Muslim units. Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware that the HVO order was basically that all army of Bosnia-Herzegovina units in certain provinces should be subordinated to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, but what I'm interested in is the following: These orders were not carried out. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That we cannot say. The HVO sought to carry them out. They were not carried out, if by that you mean they were not implemented officially with the concurrence of the Bosnian government. We know there was no concurrence. We discussed that, Izetbegovic's denunciation of the defence minister's statement, but there was an attempt by the HVO to unilaterally effectuate the orders that they gave themselves, because in effect they were telling themselves what to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us where and when? Where and when did the HVO unilaterally try to implement these orders?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They tried to do it via their actions in ethnic cleansing on the ground, which we've discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And could you tell us, Mr. Okun, the following -- in fact, we are discussing orders here that refer to the resubordination of ABiH units to the HVO command. These are the orders we are discussing here, and my question is: Where and when did the HVO take any steps in order to implement this order?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You -- you mean two subordinate the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Well, I can't give you the exact date and place, but we know of the actions they took. What they wrote on paper was one thing, and what they did on the ground was another.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Okun, if you say that you are aware of the actions they took, the only thing that is of importance to us in this courtroom is to know when and where. I'm only asking you for facts. If you can't be more precise, just say so.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm giving you the facts. You will recall the lengthy meeting between the Bosnian Croat and the Bosnian Muslim sides in Sarajevo and Zagreb. We've discussed that thoroughly. Those are facts, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Okun, those aren't facts that might prove that the HVO took action to disarm the ABiH, to expel it from Croatian provinces or to resubordinate it to its command. That is the order that we are discussing, and I would ask you to answer the question as to where and when action was taken in order to effectuate that order.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, the actions on the ground, which were the intense subject of meetings at all levels of the international conference give the answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us which actions on the ground you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The -- the cleansing operations in Gornji Vakuf was one.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's move on. What was the second one?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: A second cleansing operation? Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Some other operations, some other action taken to implement this order. Mr. Okun, please, we are discussing the order according to which the ABiH should be resubordinated to the HVO. This involves disarming, expulsion from Croatian provinces. Have a look at the order we are discussing; and we're discussing the matter of implementing the order. Where and when was any action taken in order to carry out these orders? On the basis of your answers the conclusion I can draw is you don't know.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is an incorrect --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If you don't know, that's probably because no such action was taken?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's an incorrect conclusion, Counsel. I must state that quite clearly for the benefits of the Chamber. I have said to you that the actions speak louder than the words. I've said that before. I say it again. And you can put anything on paper. Joseph Stalin used to say, "Bumaga dopuskjet" [phoen], "paper will tolerate anything." The actions were what concerned us.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Okun, and that is why I'm asking you about actions. When and where did the HVO disarm members of the ABiH? When did they expel them from Croatian provinces? And we are discussing the ABiH. Or when did they do anything to forcibly and unilaterally implement this order dated the 15th of January, 1993? We are only interested in action taken.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did that by the totality of their actions in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Okun, the conclusion I can draw is that you can't answer my question precisely. Can you at least tell us when the conflict in Central Bosnia broke out?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was, of course, always small actions here and there, cases of random and occasional violence, but the major actions broke out, to use your words, the major actions broke out after the middle of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel Alaburic, as far as the time granted to you is concerned, so far the Defence has used up six hours and 40 minutes, which means that in theory, Counsel Nozica and Counsel Murphy, who have requested one hour and 20 minutes should now take the floor, unless they have granted some of their time to you. Ms. Nozica, what is your position?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague, Senka, has just granted me five minutes, and, Your Honours, would it be possible to have an additional minutes or two since there are certain details I would like to clarify and I would like to move on very rapidly, if I could.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Okun, on a number of occasions you mentioned Prozor in October 1992 and you mentioned it as an example of wide-ranging action of ethnic cleansing in the Prozor area? Do you remember that? A minute ago you mentioned Prozor as an example of ethnic cleansing committed by the Croats. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Have a look at the bundle of documents I provided you. P 00744. I haven't got sufficient time to show you documents on the causes and reasons for the conflict in Prozor, but I would like you to have a look at a document that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: That the Muslims from Prozor drafted. It's an information dated the 14th of November, 1992. Have a look at item 2, the last part of item 2, which reads as follows -- and before the quote, and I'd like to point out that this conflicted lasted for one day; it was on the 23rd of October, 1992. And now I'll read part the of the document out. "At the time of the shelling there was no significant damage inflicted on the buildings apart from those that were specific targets. We also know that during the attack there were no civilian victims. After the artillery attack, the withdrawal commenced (on the 24th of October). Withdrawal of the civilians and soldiers commenced from the town, through the south exit." And in brackets it says, "in the direction of Jablanica." "During the retreat of units one of our soldiers got killed. Around 1200 hours the Croat forces entered Prozor." Mr. Okun, is that the fierce HVO attack launched on Prozor, the attack you've been referring to, or are you referring to some other event we're note familiar in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me whose document is this that you were reading Counsel? Who wrote those words? Whose document is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This is a document drafted by Muslims from Prozor. They had gathered in the forum of the expelled Muslim organisations. It's a document used by the Prosecution in the part of the case that concerned Prozor. I didn't want to show you HVO documents because I didn't want you to doubt their authenticity. So my question is as follows: When you mention Prozor, when you mention the very heavy operation of ethnic cleansing, are you referring to that attack or some other attack that we in the courtroom are not familiar with?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In fairness to the witness, the witness should be also referred to the next paragraph, number 3, item number 3 immediately following the end of paragraph -- section 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours. Your Honours, this is something that my colleague Scott can do during redirect, and I'll be very happy to listen to this witness's answers to any other questions, but at this point in time all I'm interested is, in the intensity of the attack.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And to deal with Prozor rapidly, Mr. Okun, I would like to tell you that in the indictment in which charges have been levelled against my client, the attack on the village of Paljike is also mention and in that attack two individuals were killed and the indictment states that in November 1992, after the negotiations of the organs of the government of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and the ABiH the civilians returned to Prozor this is paragraph 50 of the current indictment. Sir, is that the example of intensive ethnic cleansing that you have referred to here on five or six occasions?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I answer?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last sentence reads: "About 1200 hours the Croat forces entered Prozor." That's after 1200 that the cleansing started and began, and now I can understand why you did not wish to show it. That's perfectly clear. But that document you've shown me, and this one we're looking -- Counsel --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Okun --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're silencing me once again. Let the record show that you have silenced me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Okun, I'm asking you to be fair now and to see that before that sentence on the Croatian forces entering around 1200 hours it says that after the attack the civilian population and the ABiH withdrew from the town. So that means that they left Prozor before the HVO entered Prozor. That is what I wanted to show to you, but the Judges are familiar with the document, and we can move on now. Mr. Okun --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Counsel; it does not say what you said it said. It actually says the civilians and soldiers started to retreat. I repeat, started to retreat. It does not say they retreated or they finished their retreat.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: They say when the retreat started, and they said in the course of the retreat one soldiers was killed. The retreat started at night, and the HVO entered Prozor on the following day at 1200 hours. Mr. Okun, let's move on to the next subject. You also mentioned as an example of ethnic cleansing some wartime events in April 1993. General Praljak attempted to determine whether you also familiar with crimes committed against the Croats, as you seem to be familiar with the crimes apparently committed against Muslims, but I would like as though you a -- a decision, P 02078. We have already discussed this. This is a joint statement signed by Mate Boban and Alija Izetbegovic on the 25th of April, 1993, immediately after midnight. This is a document that was drafted after a meeting that you yourself attended, and in that document, under item 5, the following is stated -- it's in the middle of the paragraph. "According to the information we have to date, both sides are responsible for violations of international humanitarian law, and they undertake to urgently carry out investigations into each and every case of such violations." Mr. Okun, given that you were at that meeting, is it certain that in April 1993 there were conflicts -- there was a conflict between two armies, and the HVO and ABiH were involved, and both sides were equally responsible for all the events, and that also includes the crimes committed in the course of that fighting?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already stated -- well, with respect to April 24th, yes, I was there. I'm well aware of the meeting. I've also stated that there were no angels. You have the statement of Lord Owen saying there are no innocent parties in this. Yes, of course there were reciprocal actions, but the level of activity, the massive damage was done by the HVO and the Bosnian Croat side, and I would simply recall for you in this respect the United Nations Security Council Resolutions which denounced the Bosnian Croat activity at this time. I realise you hold up your hand because it's unwelcome for you to hear that, but I think it's important that I say it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Okun, I'm glad to hear whatever you have to say since this is really based on good and very balanced information. Tell me, do you know how many members the ABiH had in January 1993?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the ABiH had six times the amount of soldiers that the HVO had?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At all times the HVO was better equipped and, one must say, better led than the ABiH. The preponderance of numbers has to be seen in the entire picture of the fighting throughout Bosnia, and one would need to go through the entire orders of battle and deployments, which we certainly won't do, in order to -- to arrive at an answer to your question. So to answer the question specifically whether they had 6 times or 600 times doesn't really get to the point.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: According to which military doctrine is the number of soldiers in the field an irrelevant factor? But I won't ask you about that. We haven't got time to go into that. Let's sum up. Mr. Okun, are you familiar with an area in Bosnia-Herzegovina that was under the control of the ABiH, the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, at the beginning of your involvement in Bosnia and Herzegovina and at the end of your involvement in Bosnia and Herzegovina? Was that area, was that territory augmented? Did it diminish or did it remain as it had been? And when I ask you about that it's in relation to the HVO. When you have a look at the territory in relation to the HVO, not in relation to the Republika Srpska. That you could only have three possible answers. I apologise, four.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you tell me what my answers are?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: No, no. All I want to say is that you can answer this very briefly since my time has already run out.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the areas behind the confrontation line with the Bosnian Serbs were chequer-board, one might say, chequer-board, smaller areas with this or that army or sometimes Territorial Defence held control. I think you can understand that. So that the question whether and at what time these areas behind the confrontation line with the Serbs, how they changed over time, they did change over time, yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. But Mr. Okun, my question was how it changed. At the time when you were involved in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the territory under the control of the BH army, did it increase at the expense of territory and decrease under the control of the HVO until then?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some areas -- in some areas the HVO -- the ABH area increased. In the areas of concern to the HVO, their areas increased. There was, of course, much back and forth because we're talking about a war. We're talking about combat operations where one naturally has a changing picture even from day-to-day.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: That's quite so, but, Mr. Okun, let us go from the individual to the more general. Let us try and make a summary conclusion. Let us look at the whole. If we sum up the entire territory under the control of the ABiH, did it increase while you were involved with Bosnia-Herzegovina at the expense of the HVO? Or in other words, did the intensity of combat operations of the BH army increase during 1993?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, for the record, I just wish to say that I did not complete my cross-examination, but I have to end there. In any event, thank you for giving me some additional time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the transcript, we gave you 20 minutes more. It is now 1.00. We are going to have a one-hour break, which will allow Counsel Nozica and the other counsel to prepare, and we will resume in exactly one hour's time. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.59 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. I give the floor to Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: By way of introduction, my name is Peter Murphy, and with my colleague Ms. Senka Nozica, we represent Mr. Bruno Stojic. I will have a few questions for you, as well Ms. Nozica, but hopefully we won't take too long. First of all, Mr. Okun, have you ever met Mr. Stojic?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: You've never had any conversation with him as far as you recall?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never had any conversation with him as far as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And you've never, I take it, then, entered into any correspondence with him?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I'd like to begin by referring you back to paragraph 6 of your witness statement, which you have read to us before. Do you have that in front of you still?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: It seems to me, Ambassador, listening to your evidence for the last few days that probably because of your long experience as a diplomat you place a high value on precision of language. Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I try to. I'm sure I'm as imperfect a human being as anybody else, but I try to be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: That's my impression, too, and when I look at paragraph 6 of your statement, I would like to ask you about just one particular phrase that you use in describing the Bosnian Croat war aims, and about halfway down the paragraph you say one of the aims was "To erect and maintain a separate Bosnian Croat political entity (Herceg-Bosna), which could eventually unite with the Republic of Croatia, formally or informally." And with that precision of language, when you refer to an entity that could eventually unite with the Republic of Croatia, I take it you're referring there to a political process?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, formally or informally. Yes. A political process that could have evolved over time. I didn't go into it all here. The Bosnian Croats, for example, would speak of a special relationship sometimes. So there were various formulations which I tried to summarise in the three words "formally or informally."

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes. And today I think at one point you described Croatia, and indeed Serbia. As being, so to speak, the mother countries of the two groups within Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is how the Bosnian Croats saw Croatia and how the Bosnian Serbs saw Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Now, just focusing for a moment, then, on the -- the creation of the community, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, do you recall that that community was brought into existence during November of 1991?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall, but it was not of primary concern to us in November 1991. Mr. Vance and I were overwhelmingly occupied with -- with Croatia itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I understand. My question is just to establish that as -- as a chronology. You would agree with me that was the time frame in which it was created?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: At that point in time there were already in existence some of the Serbian autonomous regions; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: No, in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were self-proclaimed autonomous regions in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And these self-proclaimed Serbian regions pre-dated the formation of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna by a short time?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were almost simultaneous, but I think they probably did pre-date it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Then moving forward a little, we come to April of 1992, some four to five months later, and that is the period when the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina is recognised as an independent state by the European Union and then by the United States?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, April 6 and April 7, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: So when the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was established, we can agree that it was not established on the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina as an independent state?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The original establishment was on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina was not on that of a recognised international state; however, it was on the territory of the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina which had declared its independence from the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Now, you, sir, are a -- you told us, I think, on the first day of your testimony that you have in the past lectured on international law at Yale University?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Presently you teach at Johns Hopkins, I believe?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I should add, I'm not a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: No, I understand. But I think you mentioned to us that the course which you teach does encompass international law?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And in addition to that, throughout a very long and distinguished professional career, you have been involved in the practical application of public international law as a diplomat?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've been fortunate to negotiate numerous treaties during my time of service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Now, at the time when the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was establish, the -- it was in the general period when the Bosnian Serbs had been and were exercising force against or attacking the Republic of Croatia from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from Bosnia and from Serbia, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Now, as someone who has had a long and active involvement in the diplomatic field, have you had occasion to come across a system for diagnosing whether a state -- well, let me back up. Before I get to that, based on your long experience in international law, first of all, would you agree with me that in more traditional international law, before an entity could be regarded as a state it had to possess certain characteristics.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Control of territory, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes. Control of its borders. Having a government that functioned. Wouldn't that be right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And if the state then demonstrated over a period of time that it had those characteristics, it would gradually become recognised by other members of the international community?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but there were many exceptions to that rule also, as I'm sure you're aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes. And you're also aware that in more modern times the practice has been for statehood to be conferred more directly by the process of recognition by other states?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the more common practice. Again, it's not always the case. Witness the current situation in Kosovo, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes. And of course I also understand that a large number of states have purported to recognise Palestine, but, as we know, that's not generally accepted?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And on that same point if I may mention, Mr. Murphy, which is very relevant, when the state of Israel was created in 1947 and then proclaimed its independence, it did not control its territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But was recognised instantaneously by the Soviet Union and the United States in May 1948. Just to make the point that you're making that I'm agreeing with that there are all kinds of flexibilities involved in recognition.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes. And it's true to say also, isn't it, that even if a state is recognised it may still not function efficiently as a state?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And it may attract what has become known in international law in more recent times the status of being a failed state?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The expression "failed state" is not an official term, but it is an accurate description of certain states.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Okun, I think of in front of you yet more documents, I'm afraid. This time in this distinctive Stojic Defence pink colour. Do you have that binder in front of you?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And I would like you to just direct your attention, please, to one document, the very -- it should be the first one in the bundle. The number is 2D 00440. It should be the first document after the index.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And it should be headed "The Fund for Peace: Failed States Index 2006." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Right. And Their Honours should also have a copy of this. First of all, are you familiar with the Fund for Peace?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a general, way. I believe it's an American non-governmental organisation. I would not claim any extensive familiarity with it, but I've seen the name certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And there's a reference there to what is the acronym C-A-S-T for CAST. Have you ever come across that before?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, perhaps -- since we don't have very much time, perhaps for now you would accept it from me, and I will be corrected if I'm wrong, that what this document does is to describe what is -- what the fund for peace known calls a failed states index. You're not -- have you come across that before?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is the first time I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: So you wouldn't know, for example, that a number of governments, including the American government's now making use of this system for political analysis purposes?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never heard -- I deal extensively with the American government officially and unofficially. I've never heard anybody refer to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me -- I don't need to go into great detail then about it since -- but I would just like to ask you as someone who has great experience in this area to -- to just help me make -- to assume with me for a moment that we can use this system to make some judgements about a state, and you'll see about halfway down the page a reference to 12 indicators. Do you see that in rather small print?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And I will represent to you that these indicators are what the fund uses to make an analysis of the status of a state as being a failed state, and you can see underneath, we don't need to go through the details but they have a list of different states analysed under all these 12. I'd just like to ask you a few questions about these various indicators, and I want to focus particularly on a certain period between April of 1992 and going forward to, let us say, the end of 1993. I don't really need to go beyond that. Can we focus on that period then?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: The first of these indicators is what it calls mounting demographic pressures. And again if we had the web site up we could get more information about what that means, but -- but basically it means that there are a lot of pressures between conflicting groups of the population which can result in conflict over such things as disputes over land, property, and so on. We could agree, could we not, that that indicator would certainly be very characteristic of Bosnia and Herzegovina during the period that I mentioned?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: You wouldn't agree.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because Bosnia-Herzegovina did not have a large population at all. Before the war it was a bit under 4 million. It -- because of the invasion and the fighting and the hundreds of thousands of refugees that have been referred to earlier by Mr. Karnavas and other members of the Defence, there were many fewer. I don't think there are 4 million today, actually, but that was by no means a large or too large a number of people residing in the -- in an area the size of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So one could not speak of demographic pressures in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, I didn't mean demographic pressures in the sense that there were too many people. What -- the sense that I was trying to convey was that there were different groups of the population in conflict with each other about such things as disputes over land, property, and so on?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: In that sense.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Second indicator is a massive movement of refugees or internally displaced persons, IDP, as it's abbreviated there, which results in humanitarian emergencies. We can agree that during the period that was certainly happening, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: The third one is a legacy of vengeance, different groups seeking grievance or seeking revenge against each other because of long-standing grievance. That's certainly true, is it not?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true of the Serbs by and large. It was not true of the Muslims. And by and large not true of the Bosnian Croats. They -- they did not talk about redressing old grievances the Serbs did constantly. Mladic, General Mladic, just for example, one sentence, would always tell me that he was born in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that his father was a Bosnian and that his family had been killed during the Nazis, fascists during the Second World War, that sort of thing. But that was very common with the Serbs but not with the Muslims or Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: You could get back to the Battle of the Field of Blackbirds after just a few minutes' conversation, couldn't you?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'd prefer not to. I'm sure you would -- you wouldn't want me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: In discussions with Bosnian Serbs that would not be uncommon?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no absolutely in discussion with the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: The fourth indicator is what it calls chronic and sustained human flight. The tendency, that is, of those who can - the professionals, intellectuals and those who may fear persecution and ill-treatment - tendency for them to leave the country and be displaced can we agree that was so?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Remarkably enough that was not happening. It was quite surprising how many of the intellectuals, for example, and journalists and lawyers and professional people remained in Sarajevo during the intense Soviet -- sorry, Serbian - that's a real lapsus lingue - during the intense Serbian shelling of the city and in other places as well. That was indeed one of the noticeable aspects, was the desire of people in the main, all of them, to stay where they were. So that was not characteristic of the fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me move on, then, from that. The next one is uneven economic development along group lines. In other words, certain segments of the population might have grievances about perceived inequality of the distribution of wealth and opportunity.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not a factor either. The Bosnian Muslims and the Croats -- well, the Muslims were the most urbanised of the three people. The Serbs were the most rural. The Croats were something in between. But they -- there was -- there was no great economic disparity among the three groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: All right. Sharp or severe economic decline.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That occurred once the fighting began. Before the fighting began Bosnia was doing fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: But by the time the war got under way there was indeed a very sharp economic decline, was there not?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes and no. There were areas where the food supply was reduced. Sarajevo, for example, because of the Serbian siege. We had to fly in food to Sarajevo. But in the rest of the country one could go into small towns and go into the local restaurant and get a meal without any trouble.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Number 7 is the criminalisation or delegitimisation of the state, which appears to mean a loss of popular confidence in state institutions, the tendency towards corruption or the collapse of governmental institutions. That was certainly true, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, that tended to occur and was a particular Bosnian Serb talking point. They asserted that -- constantly, you know, that there was no such thing as Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes. Number 8, the progressive deterioration of public services. We could agree on that, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they held up pretty well all things considered, remarkably well, the public services. Again Sarajevo is the best example. Here's the capital city besieged for months with an average shell count per day of 5.000. We had UN observers in the city and on the hills, and the average number of Serbian shells falling on Sarajevo was 5.000 per day, and yet, in spite of that, the water system - very important, the water and sewage system, you can imagine vital to the city - was maintained with difficulty and with foreign assistance, but the water and sewage system functioned during the entire Serb siege.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: All right. I have a lot to go into that but for reasons of time we'll go on. Number 9, widespread violation of human rights?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Number 10, the security apparatus or a security apparatus operating as a state within a state, private armies or --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we've already discussed the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the Bosnian Serb territorial militia, that they had taken over. But I would not call it a security apparatus as a state within a state. That's something quite -- really quite different. I mean there you're talking about the NKVD or -- in Russia, or the Ministry of State Security in the old German Democratic Republic, or countries of that ilk. That did not happen in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: All right. Number 11, the rise of factionalised elites. In other words, different groups --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's another interesting point, because one might have expected that, but as I had mentioned earlier in answer to another question about the legacy of vengeance, by and large that did not happen in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say the journalists in Oslobodjenje, for example, in Sarajevo, Serbs, Croats, and -- and Muslims by and large held together and -- and sought to maintain the multi-ethnic Bosnia. Haris Silajdzic, surely an elite, the very Muslim deputy Foreign Minister in the Bosnian government, was passionate on the subject of non-factionalising the elites even as he supported the Muslim position. So that was a more complex picture but basically they held together. That was one of the encouraging aspects of the situation in what was generally a depressing picture during 1992 and 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: One of the reasons it was a depressing picture, though, was because of the amount of political rhetoric along ethnic lines. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that happens, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And finally number 12, the intervention of other states or external actors, and that certainly occurred, did it not?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the reason I've taken so long to go through those indicators with you is to try to establish if we could, and to ask you to agree with this proposition, that between April of 1992 and the end of 1993, even though Bosnia and Herzegovina was a recognise state, it was for all practical purposes a failed state.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I explain why? Briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The country had been invaded and was occupied 70 per cent of the country by the Bosnian Serbs. That doesn't make it a failed state any more than France between 1940 and '44 was a "failed state." It was occupied by the German army. They fought a war. Unfortunately, they didn't do very well, and so the German army occupied the country. That's not at all consistent with the concept of a failed state.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, let's look at what was going on. I think you've testified that President Izetbegovic had what I think you called a dual function. They may not be your exact words.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: On the other hand he was representing himself to be the representative of the Independent State of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: On the other hand, he was attending the negotiations with which you were involved, representing what we might call the Muslim side as the head of that delegation.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, but when you say he was representing himself to be the president of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that's not quite right. He was the president of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: All right. He was the president. But --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But as I -- you're quite right. He took the Muslim position, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: At the same time, a member of his government, a colleague within the government, Mr. Akmadzic, who held ministerial office, was a member of what we could call an opposing delegation at those same talks.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like not to think of it as an opposing delegation, but certainly a different delegation and different from the Muslim delegation, yes. He sat with the Croats and represented the Croat position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't hide that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: No. Well, exactly my point. It was all out there in the open that within the -- the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina there were different factions who were trying to achieve a different ultimate result.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And partly as a result of that, and partly because of difficult conditions in Sarajevo, I would suggest to you that the government in Sarajevo was effectively unable to provide services to its constituents throughout the state.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's true, that the government didn't -- I've mentioned that the Serb army controlled 70 per cent, roughly 70 per cent, of the state. Therefore, ipso facto, the Bosnian government did not control 70 per cent and could not provide the services. This was a country at war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, we -- the next step that I want to take, Mr. Okun, from -- from there is to suggest to you that in those very difficult circumstances any group, but since we're talking about the Bosnian Croats, let's talk about them, throughout the period that I've mentioned, between April of 1992 and the end of 1993, was entitled to take action to organise themselves for the purpose of survival, defence, and providing for their everyday legitimate needs?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up to a point, yes. Beyond a certain point, no. Of course every group had the right of self-defence. It's Article 51 of the United Nations Charter. It's enshrined in international law; there's no question about self-defence. But what the Bosnian Serbs did and what the Bosnian Croats did went well beyond that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I'm just dealing now with what the entitlement was. I think we can all agree that on the ground on all sides of this conflict things happened that should not have happened.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: But I'm looking now as a broad picture. Let me explain why I'm putting this question to you. You've represented to the Trial Chamber that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna represents an attempt essentially to set up an entity, a political entity with the ultimate goal in some manner of being incorporated with or being annexed by the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: What I'm suggesting to you is that, as a matter of public international law and as a matter of the facts that were prevailing during this period, there is in fact an alternative explanation for the existence of that entity, which has nothing whatsoever to do with territorial claims but is, rather, associated with defence and the practical need to survive in time of war.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It went beyond that, sir. If that is where it had stopped there would be no dispute, but we have had examples of the Bosnian Serbs and the Bosnian Croats telling us, talking to us about their desires for the future territorial composition of the state that went way beyond self-defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Let's work with that assumption for a moment. Let's suppose that's right. You're familiar with the expression, "hindsight is 20/20." I'm not sure -- that's probably not going to translate into French or B/C/S. Let me rephrase it. It's a mistake to look at history backwards from the present time. Would you agree? We have to try and put ourselves in the position of the people who were there at the time.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And to understand how things looked to them.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And would you not agree with me that during the period that I've been referring to there was, to say the very least, a serious doubt as to whether the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina could survive?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was both a serious doubt given the invasion and the fighting, and also a serious hope on the part unquestionably of the Bosnian Serbs and to a lesser degree on the part of the Bosnian Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, if -- if you were in that position, I mean, you're --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Please excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Please, Your Honour. Please do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You said there was a hope. In which way? What are you saying they hoped for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They hoped to be able to link their political entities, Republika Srpska for the Bosnian Serbs, Herceg-Bosna for the Bosnian Croats. They wanted to link their entities with their mother countries when they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm very grateful, because I want to confront that head-on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Let's assume that's true. In the context of a dissolving state which the former Yugoslavia was, we can agree, and in the situation of chaos that Bosnia and Herzegovina represented during that period, I suggest to you that both legally and in every other way there is nothing inherently illegitimate in that proposition.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I'm afraid you're wrong there, Counsel, because what has been brought out by numerous questions, territorial integrity does manner -- matter. Bosnia and Herzegovina was a sovereign state within recognised international borders. So to say that chaos represented during that period, I suggest to you that legally and every other way there was nothing inherently illegitimate in that proposition. I can't agree with that. It is inherent from beginning -- inherently illegitimate from beginning to end to take advantage of a wartime situation to set up alternate states.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, that wasn't quite what I was suggesting, but let's -- let's just pursue it for a moment.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: You've made the equation between -- or drawn a comparison between the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna on the one hand and Republika Srpska on the other.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Now, to the extent that the Bosnian Serbs wanted to create an entity that eventually might lead to incorporation into or some relationship with Serbia, the simple fact of the matter is that they have succeeded, at least in part, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Because today Republika Srpska, as we know, is an entity within Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: That arrangement was the result of an internationally brokered agreement.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Dayton framework accord.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And it was internationally brokered because those who were conducting those negotiations realised that it reflected a certain reality with which they had to deal.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a very long story. I could go into it. I'm sure you don't want me to. There are many reasons why it was recognise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: That's true. But the fact is that with international approval, however in some ways reluctant, it was so recognised.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was recognised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And is recognised today.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Now, one thing you -- you worked long and hard, and I'm not sure anybody has said this in -- I don't think Mr. Scott did, but in case nobody has, we all appreciate the long work you put in with Lord Owen and Mr. Vance to try and solve this situation, but one thing puzzles me about the -- the evidence that you've given about the Vance-Owen agreement. You've said repeatedly that the proposal was not ethnically based. Is that -- am I right? You've said that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I have -- what I've said, Mr. Murphy, was that the composition of the provinces to the maximum degree were not ethnically based, and we've discussed that extensively. You know, how many people lived -- lived where. I've also said that the important aspects of the plan were to reverse ethnic cleansing and to maintain to the maximum degree possible the overall multi-ethnic nature of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. One, of course, had to take into account the fact that certain people lived in certain places. We were not drawing maps on the moon, and that, of course, accounted for anomalous situations. And one of the previous counsels asked me to look at the provinces and, you know, where were the Serbs, et cetera. But the essence was to maintain a multi-ethnic state which Bosnia and Herzegovina had been in, let us say, 1990, to the maximum degree possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You ought to slow down a little because they are behind with the transcript, and I'm afraid something might get lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. I was for a while listening in French as I usually do, but I couldn't hear the ambassador so I switched back to English. I apologise for that. I'll try again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: You said this morning, for example, that in case of uncertainty where you had a mixed Croat-Muslim area, that you tended to give what you called the benefit of the doubt to the Croats.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And that does indicate, doesn't it, that essentially the drawing of the boundaries between the cantons or the provinces was, in fact, ethnically based?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not ethnically based. There were other factors, Mr. Murphy, that we had to take into account, and that's so stated in the plan discussing the structure of the provinces. Of course the people who lived there counted, but also the geography. Where were the mountains? Where were the valleys? What was the industrial base inside that canton? What about the power lines and the power grids? So a multiplicity of factors had to be taken into account, and were taken into account. Now, it was a complex situation. For example, just to get directly to your point, the Muslim majority provinces had the best part of the industry of the industrial base of pre-war Bosnia-Herzegovina. And it was not a large industrial base, but as we've discussed here there were major industrial installations. The only jet factory in all of Yugoslavia was located in Sarajevo, for example. We've discussed Novi Travnik, and things like that. The point I just want to make in answer to your question about benefit of the doubt was that we knew from our own map and from our experts that the Muslims were going to receive a very good industrial base, and we wanted to be fair to the Bosnian Croats to make sure that in other ways they were compensated. Just as in the same case the Bosnian Serbs under the map of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan had -- in geographic terms, 43 per cent of the entire country were in Bosnian Serb majority provinces, but as Mr. Buha said, "You've given us the snakes and the rocks and the stones." They were the poorest areas of the country. So that in drawing the map, which was a difficult business, as everybody knows, many factors had to be taken into account, and the negotiators did their best.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Just one short matter finally, Ambassador. Can I ask whether you have read the indictment in the present case?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it some months ago. I have not read it recently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I think that's all I have. Thank you. My colleague Ms. Nozica has a few questions. Thank you very much, Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ambassador, my name is Senka Nozica, and I'm an attorney from Sarajevo. Over the past four days you have shown an enviable level of knowledge about Bosnia-Herzegovina, its territory, and the whole of the Balkans, in fact. You have shown us that you remember a great deal of things, that you have an exceptionally good memory, but you also demonstrated that you had a lot of information available to you, and because of that latter, I'd like to tell you as somebody who spent the entire war in Sarajevo, linked to your answer in response to my colleague's question about the communal system, you said that the observers from Sarajevo told you that this communal system, in addition to the 5.000 shells a day, was kept going, the utility system and the communal system. And I'd just like to tell you that the citizens of Sarajevo on average, for the four years of war, did not have water, if you were to do add the days, more than two months during that whole period and an equal amount of electricity. There was water in just three or four points in town, and it was very dangerous to go there, and we received our electricity very rarely, so that I think, and you can accept this just as a piece of information, that your information along those lines are not completely correct and are somewhat lacking. However, I'd like to deal with some other issues now. I don't have much time at my disposal, and they are subjects touched upon by my colleague, Ms. Alaburic. I have to go back to those questions because the Prosecutor showed you at least two documents which referred to Mr. Bruno Stojic, and they are documents which deal with January 1993, and they are the documents which speak about subordination, the HVO and the BH army in both directions, vice versa, one to the other, et cetera. And during the examination-in-chief, you said in addressing those documents, and you said about those orders and decisions that they were premature?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, I never said that. Lord Owen used the word "premature." Lord Owen -- that's Lord Owen's word. If I said that word, I was quoting him. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Did you say that they were not in the spirit of the Vance-Owen Plan, that they did not reflect the spirit of the Vance-Owen Plan? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said they reflected neither the spirit nor the letter of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. And the third point. You gave these three qualifications, and you said that they led to untoward consequences, undesired consequences. Do you agree with that as being your third qualification?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made that point, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'd like to focus on the second point, this one -- especially this one order signed by my client, and linked to that order, the orders that followed, was it in the spirit and letter, as you say, of the Vance-Owen Plan? We have already had an opportunity of looking at the document today, so may we have it back on e-court. It is P 09852. That is the document number. And it is a document which is the fourth in your binder. It is green, to help you find it. And I'd like to inform you and the Chamber and the Prosecutor that I have placed all the documents that I'm going to use in the binder including the ones that have been use by the Prosecutor. Ours are pink, and the green ones are the documents that the Prosecutor used during the examination-in-chief. Have you found the document? The number of the document once again is 9852, and --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Okay. Can we take a look at page 13 together, now, please. My colleague said a moment ago, and we can find that on page 11, it is the introductory statement by Lord Owen, but as to the first paragraph on page 13 you said that they were in fact the principles laid down by Lord Owen, or paraphrased by Lord Owen in the introductory speech, if I understood you correctly. And I'm referring to the first paragraph on page 13?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we don't need Lord Owen's paraphrase. We have the text of the document, Ms. Nozica. So, you know, Lord Owen's paraphrase, Secretary Vance's paraphrase, is precisely what you call it, a paraphrase. We have the text in front of us. We don't need to paraphrase it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Ambassador, I'd like to ask you to look and see what he said about subordination, Mr. Owen that is, at this conference which was held in Geneva, linked to the matter of subordination. Now, we haven't received it from the Prosecutor, the translation of this text into the Croatian, Bosnian, Serbian language, but just in order to have the right transcript come up, could you read it out, please? Could you read the sentence out?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean what Lord Owen said?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And it begins were "Bosnian Serb forces." It's the second line. The first sentence, second line, page 13.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: To the end of the paragraph, please, if you would.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Lord Owen says, and I quote: "Bosnian Serb forces might withdraw to provinces 2, 4, 6. Bosnian Croat forces could be deployed in province 3, and the remaining forces would hopefully reach agreement as to their deployment in provinces 1, 5, 8, 9, and 10. Under our constitutional principles (number 8) Bosnia and Herzegovina is to be progressively demilitarised." End of paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. As you say, constitutional principles number 8, the eighth constitutional principle, in fact relates to demilitarisation, does it not?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume if Lord Owen says so it does. I don't have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you now take a look at page 11, which comes before this paragraph if there are any uncertainty so that we can be certain about what we're reading? Can we have a look at page 11, Annex III, the opening statement of Lord Owen. That's what it is. Is that right? Just for the transcript so we know what we're reading from.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Ambassador, can we agree that from this explanation and these qualifications made by Mr. Owen that it emerges that the armies in the provinces would suppose -- were supposed to reach an agreement about how they were going to be deployed?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is so stated in the Vance-Owen Peace Plan.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the Prosecutor read out to you part of the discussion by Mr. Izetbegovic from a meeting held in Zagreb, dated the 15th of January, 1993. And at that meeting -- well, you said you didn't attend the meeting, that you weren't there. Are you a little tired? I seem to feel that you are a little tired already. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I follow you with intense interest and even enthusiasm.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm very pleased to hear that. Thank you. So you said you were not at that meeting; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We've gone over this several times. You had the transcript. I believe I was not. I would have to consult my diaries. Unlike Mr. Karnavas, I have not read them 10.000 times. I stand -- whatever you say about the record, the record I think has already been made clear, so why don't you continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. All right. Now, may we look at the transcript? It is in my binder, and the number of the document is P 01158, and it is the sixth document from the bottom. The Prosecutor read out part of the discussion by Mr. Izetbegovic on page 18 in the English version, and it is page 48 in the Croatian version. Let me remind you, and you can believe me when I tell you that it is the portion where Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, in his own way, is seen to be a little nervous or showing dissatisfaction because he considers that the interpretation of the plan by the Bosnian Croats is not being done in the way in which the plan reads, especially about this question of subordination of the 15th of January. Now, may we take a look together at this again and see what Mr. Owen said at the meeting about this matter. And that will be found on page 52 in the Croatian version and page 20 of the English version. If you can't find it, I'll read it out.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have found it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: That's great. Thank you. Now, what he says here, and I'd like to start off from the third sentence, is this: "As far as the individual provinces are concerned, in explaining the system I said that the Serb military forces were to withdraw to Banja Luka, Bijeljina, and Eastern Herzegovina. As to the rest, I didn't offer any suggestions, but I think that I've already mentioned that this is a question which should be resolved together by the BH army and the HVO." Do you agree with me that once again Mr. Owen is suggesting that consultation and agreement be used to resolve this issue about the BH army and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's summarising section E of the Vance-Owen Plan, the one called, "the withdrawal of forces." And the line in the plan that he's summarising reads: "Both Bosnian army and HVO forces shall be deployed in provinces 5, 8, 9 and 10 under arrangements agreed between them." Yes, there was to be joint consultation about the deployment in those provinces. That's what Lord Owen meant. Of course, he didn't have the plan in front of him when he was speaking so some of the words may vary, but he's accurate. He's quite accurate in saying that the -- this was an issue for the BH army and the HVO to discuss together, yes. That's -- that's accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Ambassador. Let us now look at one of these orders which was not shown to you by the Prosecutor, and it is under number P 01140. It is number 3 from the top in your binder, and it is marked with a pink sticker. Could we please have a look at it, because I consider it to be essential because it was signed by Mr. Stojic. I wish to refer to points 1 and 5 because we've already seen some other -- the others. Let us see what it says under point 1. "The Main Staff of the forces of the HVO must immediately establish contact with all operative forces and commands of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the territory of provinces 3, 8, 10 and 1, 5, and 9 in order to make concrete the implementation of the decision." Have you found it? I see you're looking through the documents, but every word is important for me. 1140, three from the top, bearing a pink sticker. Ambassador, it's on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You've found it, I see.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So to order -- in order concreting to implement the decision of the HVO HZ, dated the 15th of January, 1993. This is the decision passed by the HVO and signed by Mr. Prlic. Now I'd ask you to look at point 5, which says: "Officers of the army of BH shall enter the command of the armed forces of the HVO at the level of operations zones and brigades in proportion to the number of soldiers that are at the front lines." And then we see at the end to whom it was addressed the Main Staff of the HVO, the staff of the army of BH, the defence minister of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the military police administration, et cetera. Now, this preamble, to the best of your understanding, I assume that you see this document for the first time, the preamble instructing the Main Staff of the armed forces should establish direct contact with all operative zones and staffs of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina for concreting implementing the decision. Doesn't this order imply an attempt at an agreement precisely in the way it is stated in the Vance-Owen Plan and its annex?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer to that question is no, and the reason for it is as follows: On the same day, in the immediately preceding document in your package, there is the decision announced by the Croatian Defence Council, the one signed by Dr. Prlic, which says as its first sentence: "All units of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina which at this moment are stationed in provinces 3, 8, and 10, which have been declared Croatian provinces in the Geneva Accords, shall be subordinated to the command of the Main Staff of the HVO forces." The item that you read descends from this document. So when it says we will -- you know, you should come and discuss with us, it was on the basis your subordination to the HVO. That's on the basis of Dr. Prlic's document that I just read. So it was not an independent, "come let's talk about matters." It was: You are subordinate to us. You report to us and now we talk.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Ambassador, I will tell you quite sincerely that I didn't expect you to give me a different answer. I kindly ask you to look through these documents together, and the conclusion will be drawn by Their Honours. The decision that was sign by Mr. Prlic is a decision, and this ask an order that operationalises that decision.
